items.q: Match the following DKA management step — 1) Fluid 2) Insulin 3) Potassium 4) Dextrose … A) 0.9% saline, switch to 0.45% if hyperNa B) 0.1 U/kg regular IV bolus then 0.1 U/kg/h C) Add KCl once K+ <5.2 mEq/L D) Add when glucose <200 mg/dL to allow continued insulin
items.exp: DKA fluids start with 0.9% saline; insulin is regular 0.1 U/kg bolus then 0.1 U/kg/h; KCl is added once K+ <5.2; dextrose is added when glucose <200 mg/dL. (Book p931)

items.q: A DKA patient on insulin infusion has glucose 190 mg/dL, K+ 4.0 mEq/L, pH 7.22 and anion gap still raised. The most appropriate next step is:
opts: Add dextrose to fluids and continue insulin
items.exp: Once glucose <200 mg/dL but anion gap is still raised, add dextrose to allow continued insulin infusion to close the gap. (Book p931)

items.q: Assess DKA fluids: I Total fluid deficit is typically 6–9 L. II The 3/3+3/9+3/12 rule (page mnemonic) structures replacement.
items.exp: Total fluid deficit is 6–9 L; the page uses a 3/3+3/9+3/12 rule (or similar) to distribute replacement. (Book p931)

items.q: Which is the odd one out — an indication for stopping IV insulin in DKA?
opts: Anion gap closure and bicarbonate >18 mEq/L with pH >7.3
Glucose <70 mg/dL with no IV dextrose
items.exp: Anion gap closure, bicarbonate >18 and pH >7.3 are criteria for resolution and transition to subcutaneous insulin; the others are not transition criteria. (Book p931)

items.q: DKA protocols typically add KCl once serum K+ falls below ___ mEq/L.
items.exp: KCl is added once K+ <5.2; if K+ <3.3, insulin should be held until replacement. (Book p931)

items.q: Match the following HHS feature — 1) Typical age 2) Plasma osmolarity 3) Glucose 4) Prognosis … A) Older T2DM patient B) 320–380 mOsm/kg C) >600 mg/dL D) Worse than DKA
items.exp: HHS occurs in older T2DM, osm 320–380, glucose >600 mg/dL and carries worse prognosis than DKA. (Book p931)

items.q: An 80-year-old with T2DM has glucose 980 mg/dL, plasma osm 360 mOsm/kg, pH 7.38 and minimal ketones. The most consistent diagnosis is:
items.exp: Severe hyperglycaemia, high osmolarity, near-normal pH and minimal ketones fit HHS. (Book p931)

items.q: Assess HHS fluid management: I 0.45% saline is often used after initial 0.9% saline. II HHS fluid deficit averages around 12 L.
items.exp: Initial 0.9% saline, often followed by 0.45% saline as Na+ normalises; HHS fluid deficit averages around 12 L. (Book p931)

items.q: Match the following DKA-vs-HHS lab — 1) Glucose 2) Osmolarity 3) Ketones 4) Anion gap … A) 350–400 vs >800 mg/dL B) 300–320 vs 320–380 mOsm/kg C) +++ vs ± D) ↑ vs N/↓
items.exp: DKA: glucose 350–400, osm 300–320, ketones +++, AG raised. HHS: glucose >800, osm 320–380, ketones ±, AG normal or low. (Book p931)

items.q: An SGLT2-inhibitor user has glucose 220 mg/dL with ketoacidosis. The most consistent diagnosis is:
items.exp: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycaemic DKA with glucose <250 mg/dL; recognition requires a high index of suspicion. (Book p931)

items.q: Euglycaemic DKA is most commonly associated with ___ use.
items.exp: SGLT2 inhibitors are the classical cause of euglycaemic DKA. (Book p931)

items.q: Assess transition off IV insulin: I Subcutaneous insulin should overlap the IV infusion by 1–2 hours. II Bicarbonate correction is routine.
items.exp: Overlap subcutaneous insulin with IV for 1–2 hours to prevent rebound ketoacidosis; bicarbonate is reserved for severe acidaemia (pH <6.9). (Book p931)
